::: {.route-question}
Question for today: CPM assumes unlimited crews. What happens to CellCo's 20.67-week plan when one installation crew must do both F and G?
:::

## When resources are limited {#resources}

::: {.two}
::: {}
F (install containers, 2.0 weeks) and G (install power conversion, 3.17 weeks) both need CellCo's only specialist installation crew.

In the CPM schedule they overlap: G runs from week 14.83 to 18.00, F from 16.50 to 18.50. With one crew, one must wait for the other.
:::
::: {}
```{=html}
<table class="wide" style="white-space:nowrap">
  <thead><tr><th>Schedule, weeks</th><th class="num">G</th><th class="num">F</th><th class="num">Finish</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Unlimited crews (CPM)</td><td class="num">14.83–18.00</td><td class="num">16.50–18.50</td><td class="num">20.67</td></tr>
    <tr><td>One crew, G first</td><td class="num">14.83–18.00</td><td class="num">18.00–20.00</td><td class="num hit">22.17</td></tr>
    <tr><td>One crew, F first</td><td class="num">18.50–21.67</td><td class="num">16.50–18.50</td><td class="num">23.83</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
```
:::
:::

::: {.bridge}
Even the better sequence adds **1.5 weeks** that the CPM schedule does not show. A resource conflict can create a new critical path.
:::

## See the schedule {#gantt-explorer data-hold="true"}

```{=html}
<div class="widget" id="gx">
  <div class="w-controls"><span class="w-toggle" role="group" aria-label="Schedule">
    <button type="button" data-m="cpm" aria-pressed="true">Unlimited crews</button><button type="button" data-m="gf" aria-pressed="false">One crew, G first</button><button type="button" data-m="fg" aria-pressed="false">One crew, F first</button></span></div>
  <svg id="gx-svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 330" role="img" aria-label="Gantt chart of the installation project under the chosen schedule"></svg>
  <div class="w-readout" id="gx-out" aria-live="polite"></div>
</div>
<script>
(function () {
  const root = document.getElementById('gx'); if (!root) return;
  root.addEventListener('click', (e) => e.stopPropagation());
  const te = { A: 20 / 6, B: 4.5, C: 52 / 6, D: 5, E: 7, F: 2, G: 19 / 6, H: 13 / 6 };
  const pred = { A: [], B: ['A'], C: ['B'], D: ['A'], E: ['B'], F: ['C', 'D'], G: ['D', 'E'], H: ['F', 'G'] };
  function sched(m) {
    const pr = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(pred));
    if (m === 'gf') pr.F.push('G');
    if (m === 'fg') pr.G.push('F');
    const ES = {}, EF = {}, keys = Object.keys(te);
    while (Object.keys(EF).length < keys.length) {
      for (const k of keys) {
        if (k in EF || !pr[k].every((q) => q in EF)) continue;
        ES[k] = Math.max(0, ...pr[k].map((q) => EF[q])); EF[k] = ES[k] + te[k];
      }
    }
    return { ES, EF };
  }
  function draw(m) {
    const { ES, EF } = sched(m), W = 1160, L = 60, R = 20, X = (t) => L + t / 25 * (W - L - R);
    let g = '';
    for (let t = 0; t <= 25; t += 5) g += `<line x1="${X(t)}" x2="${X(t)}" y1="0" y2="300" stroke="#B9C1C6"/><text x="${X(t)}" y="322" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#333F4A">${t}</text>`;
    Object.keys(te).forEach((k, i) => {
      const y = 6 + i * 36, crew = k === 'F' || k === 'G';
      g += `<text x="${L - 12}" y="${y + 22}" text-anchor="end" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1C242B">${k}</text>`;
      g += `<rect x="${X(ES[k])}" y="${y + 4}" width="${X(EF[k]) - X(ES[k])}" height="26" rx="3" fill="${crew ? '#E29A2D' : '#0F6E6B'}" opacity="${crew ? 1 : 0.8}"/>`;
      g += `<text x="${X(EF[k]) + 6}" y="${y + 22}" font-size="15" fill="#333F4A">${ES[k].toFixed(2)}–${EF[k].toFixed(2)}</text>`;
    });
    g += `<line x1="${X(EF.H)}" x2="${X(EF.H)}" y1="0" y2="300" stroke="#BE654C" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>`;
    document.getElementById('gx-svg').innerHTML = g;
    document.getElementById('gx-out').innerHTML = `Finish: <span class="best">${EF.H.toFixed(2)} weeks</span>${m === 'cpm' ? '' : `, ${(EF.H - 20.6667).toFixed(2)} weeks later than CPM`}. Amber bars use the shared crew.`;
  }
  root.querySelectorAll('[data-m]').forEach((b) => b.addEventListener('click', () => { root.querySelectorAll('[data-m]').forEach((x) => x.setAttribute('aria-pressed', x === b)); draw(b.dataset.m); }));
  draw('cpm');
})();
</script>
```

## Activity · Sequence the crew {#act1 .activity data-hold="true"}

[Pairs · 20 minutes · squared paper]{.act-label}

::: {.prompt}
Draw the Gantt chart for one crew by hand, then check it on the previous slide.
:::

1. Which activity is ready for the crew first, F or G? When is the other one ready?
2. Draw both sequences. Which finishes earlier, and by how much?
3. CellCo can hire a second crew for G only, for CNY 0.6 million. The grid bonus pays CNY 0.5 million per week saved. Should it hire?

::: {.selfstudy}
Studying alone: answer question 3 before you go on.
:::

## Activity · Answer {#act1-answer}

::: {.two}
::: {}
G is ready first, at week 14.83 (after E). F is ready at 16.50 (after C).

"G first" finishes at **22.17 weeks**; "F first" at 23.83. Starting whichever job is ready first wins here by 1.67 weeks.
:::
::: {}
::: {.route-question}
A second crew restores the 20.67-week CPM plan, 1.5 weeks earlier than 22.17. That is worth 1.5 × 0.5 = CNY 0.75 million against a cost of 0.6, so hire it.
:::
:::
:::

## Shortest path: routing a delivery {#shortest-path}

::: {.two}
::: {}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" role="img" aria-label="Road network from port P to plant T through junctions a, b, c and d with travel times in minutes. The shortest route is P, a, c, T, 95 minutes.">
  <g font-family="Source Sans 3, sans-serif" font-size="18">
    <g stroke="#B9C1C6" stroke-width="3">
      <line x1="50" y1="150" x2="200" y2="60"/><line x1="50" y1="150" x2="200" y2="240"/><line x1="200" y1="60" x2="360" y2="60"/><line x1="200" y1="240" x2="360" y2="60"/>
      <line x1="200" y1="240" x2="360" y2="240"/><line x1="200" y1="60" x2="360" y2="240"/><line x1="360" y1="60" x2="510" y2="150"/><line x1="360" y1="240" x2="510" y2="150"/>
    </g>
    <g stroke="#E29A2D" stroke-width="6"><line x1="50" y1="150" x2="200" y2="60"/><line x1="200" y1="60" x2="360" y2="60"/><line x1="360" y1="60" x2="510" y2="150"/></g>
    <g fill="#333F4A"><text x="105" y="92">40</text><text x="105" y="222">25</text><text x="272" y="50">25</text><text x="262" y="200">50</text><text x="272" y="262">30</text><text x="262" y="116">15</text><text x="445" y="92">30</text><text x="445" y="222">45</text></g>
    <g fill="#F3F0EB" stroke="#0F6E6B" stroke-width="2.5"><circle cx="50" cy="150" r="22"/><circle cx="200" cy="60" r="22"/><circle cx="200" cy="240" r="22"/><circle cx="360" cy="60" r="22"/><circle cx="360" cy="240" r="22"/><circle cx="510" cy="150" r="22"/></g>
    <g text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700" fill="#1C242B"><text x="50" y="156">P</text><text x="200" y="66">a</text><text x="200" y="246">b</text><text x="360" y="66">c</text><text x="360" y="246">d</text><text x="510" y="156">T</text></g>
  </g>
</svg>
```
:::
::: {}
Dijkstra's algorithm labels each node with its shortest known time from P, always fixing the unvisited node with the smallest label next.

The shortest route is **P-a-c-T, 95 minutes**. Going to the nearest junction first (b, 25 minutes) leads to at best 100 minutes: nearest-first is not shortest.
:::
:::

## Maximal flow: the line's bottleneck {#max-flow}

::: {.two}
::: {}
```{=html}
<table class="wide">
  <thead><tr><th>Link</th><th class="num">Capacity, cells/h</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Source → formation F1, F2</td><td class="num">900, 600</td></tr>
    <tr><td>F1 → aging A1, A2</td><td class="num">500, 400</td></tr>
    <tr><td>F2 → aging A1, A2</td><td class="num">300, 300</td></tr>
    <tr><td>A1 → packing, A2 → packing</td><td class="num hit">700, 600</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Packing → shipping</td><td class="num">1,400</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
```
:::
::: {}
The maximal flow is **1,300 cells/h**. It equals the capacity of the minimum cut, the two links from aging to packing: 700 + 600.

Adding formation capacity buys nothing: raising F1's supply to 1,200 still gives 1,300. Raising A2 → packing to 800 lifts the flow to 1,400, where packing becomes the limit.
:::
:::

[Max-flow min-cut theorem: the largest flow through a network equals the smallest total capacity of links whose removal disconnects source from sink.]{.note-line}

## What we learned {#debrief}

::: {.takeaways}
::: {.tk}
A shared resource can lengthen a project beyond its critical path. With one crew, CellCo's plan grows from 20.67 to 22.17 weeks.
:::
::: {.tk}
Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest routes; going to the nearest node first can miss them.
:::
::: {.tk .key}
The maximal flow equals the minimum cut. Invest in the links of the cut, not elsewhere.
:::
:::
